skills.name: Small firms: roles, survival and limits

note.text: Small firms can survive through specialised demand, personal service, flexibility, local knowledge or a market too limited to support large-scale production. Size depends on the measure and context, not a universal employee cutoff supplied by this lesson. Small firms may also face weak bargaining power, limited finance and dependence on few people or customers. A firm can deliberately remain small and profitable; another can remain small because it cannot obtain resources to expand. Neither case follows from size alone.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain why a small firm may survive and calculate profit without confusing small size with failure. Builds on: growth methods and scale advantages or disadvantages. Leads to: location choices suited to the activity and its customers.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: Small firms can survive through specialised demand, personal service, flexibility, local knowledge or a market too limited to support large-scale production. Size depends on the measure and context, not a universal employee cutoff supplied by this lesson. Small firms may also face weak bargaining power, limited finance and dependence on few people or customers. A firm can deliberately remain small and profitable; another can remain small because it cannot obtain resources to expand. Neither case follows from size alone.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: An invented Buea repairer serves customers who value adjustments and direct contact. Demand may suit a small workshop rather than mass production. A large competitor may have lower standard-unit costs, while the small firm supplies a different service. These advantages require relevant skills and customers willing to pay, not just a label such as friendly business.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Link each survival explanation to demand or production conditions. Compare revenue and costs before judging profitability. Do not infer that small firms create only benefits or that every owner wants expansion. Distinguish being small from being legally a sole proprietor: a company can also be small.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: niche demand: a specialised segment of customers with particular requirements.
personal service: direct attention suited to an individual customer’s requirements.
flexibility: ability to adjust activities relatively quickly in the stated setting.
resource limitation: a shortage restricting what the firm can do or how it can expand.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: The repairer serves unusual adjustments that mass suppliers do not offer.
The owner discusses a customer’s particular repair needs.
The small workshop changes its service mix as local needs change.
The workshop cannot finance suitable additional equipment.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: niche demand: A specialised segment can be viable but still has a limited market.
personal service: Service can attract demand, but costs and willingness to pay still matter.
flexibility: Adaptation still faces capacity, skill and finance constraints.
resource limitation: Some firms remain small because constraints restrict feasible choices.

questions.prompt: A fictional specialised repair firm completes {jobs} jobs, receiving {price} CFA francs per job. Total stated costs are {cost}. Calculate accounting profit for this period.

misconceptions.explain: That is revenue before deducting costs.
That is profit per job, not for all completed jobs.

solution: Profit = revenue − total stated costs = {answer} CFA francs.
